title: The request lifecycle: guards, interceptors & filters
objectives: Predict the order guards, interceptors, pipes and the handler run in, and what each one can see
Choose a guard for admit/reject decisions and an interceptor for shaping or timing the response
Write guards that fail closed and read @Roles metadata with Reflector; throw 401 vs return false (403); register via APP_GUARD
Write interceptors that map the response, log failures with finalize, and return next.handle()
Predict the status a thrown error becomes and which single filter handles it; register via APP_FILTER

questions.prompt: A guard needs to authorize based on `dto.organizationId` from the request body. Why is that awkward?

options.text: Guards run before pipes, so the body is still raw untransformed input — there is no validated DTO yet
Guards have no access to the request at all
Guards can't be async, so they can't read a stream
The body is frozen until the handler runs

questions.explanation: The order is guards → interceptors → pipes → handler. A guard can read `switchToHttp().getRequest().body`, but it's un-whitelisted, uncoerced input, so any check on it duplicates validation. Payload-dependent authorization usually belongs in the service, where the DTO and the entity are both available.

questions.prompt: Every response must be wrapped as `{ data, requestId }`. Which component, and why not the others?

options.text: An interceptor — it's the only component that can transform the handler's return value
Middleware, since it runs for every request
An exception filter, since it writes the response
A pipe, applied to the return value

questions.explanation: `next.handle().pipe(map((data) => ({ data, requestId })))` is the canonical shape. Middleware only has `(req, res, next)` and never sees what the controller returned; a filter only runs on the error path; pipes operate on incoming arguments, not outgoing values.

questions.prompt: Your global guard takes `ConfigService` in its constructor. Which registration lets Nest's injector build it?

options.text: `{ provide: APP_GUARD, useClass: RolesGuard }` in a module's providers
`app.useGlobalGuards(new RolesGuard(config))` in main.ts
Marking the guard `@Global()`
`@UsePipes(RolesGuard)` on every controller

questions.explanation: Registering under the `APP_GUARD` token makes the guard a provider of a module, so Nest builds it with its dependencies. `useGlobalGuards` takes an instance you constructed outside any module: the injector supplies nothing, so the `config` in that option has to be fetched by hand (`app.get(ConfigService)`) and every future constructor change repeated in `main.ts`. It can work; it just isn't the injector doing it. `@Global()` applies to modules, and `@UsePipes` binds pipes, not guards. `APP_INTERCEPTOR`, `APP_FILTER` and `APP_PIPE` exist for the same reason.

questions.prompt: An auth guard returns `false` when the `Authorization` header is missing. What does the client get, and what should it get?

options.text: 403 Forbidden — but a missing credential is 401 Unauthorized, so throw `UnauthorizedException` instead
401 — and that's correct for a missing header
500, because the guard didn't throw
404, since the route is treated as non-existent

questions.explanation: `return false` produces `ForbiddenException` → 403, which tells the client "you're not allowed" when the truth is "I don't know who you are". 401 tells it to authenticate and retry; 403 tells it not to bother. Throwing the exception you mean is how you control that.

questions.prompt: A timing interceptor logs with `next.handle().pipe(tap(() => log(Date.now() - start)))`. Which requests never get logged?

options.text: Every request where the handler threw — the single-callback `tap` only observes the success notification
Requests slower than the default timeout
Only requests served from cache
None; tap sees every outcome

questions.explanation: `tap(fn)` is shorthand for the `next` handler only, so failures skip it — and failures are exactly the requests whose duration you wanted. Use the observer form `tap({ next, error })` or `finalize(...)`, which fires on success, error and unsubscribe.

questions.prompt: A controller has `@UseFilters(DomainErrorFilter)`, which is `@Catch(DomainError)`. One of its routes adds `@UseFilters(AuditAllFilter)`, a bare `@Catch()`. That route throws a `DomainError`. What handles it?

options.text: Only `AuditAllFilter` — Nest checks route filters, then controller, then global, and the first whose `@Catch` matches wins
Only `DomainErrorFilter` — Nest prefers the filter bound to the most specific exception type
Both: `AuditAllFilter` first, then `DomainErrorFilter`
Nest throws an ambiguous-filter error at boot

questions.explanation: Selection is by position, not by specificity: route-level filters are tried first, and a bare `@Catch()` matches everything, so `AuditAllFilter` wins and `DomainErrorFilter` never sees the error. Filters don't chain either: the chosen one owns the whole response, which is why a catch-all must produce a complete response itself (or extend `BaseExceptionFilter`). To keep the domain mapping on that route, narrow the route filter or bind both there — listing the catch-all first, since within one `@UseFilters()` the last one listed is tried first.

questions.prompt: A unique-constraint violation from the DB driver reaches the client as a 500. Where's the fix?

options.text: Catch the driver error where it happens, translate the known case to `ConflictException`, and rethrow anything unrecognized
Add a global `@Catch()` filter that maps any error to 409
Add an async DB uniqueness validator to the DTO so it becomes a 400
Wrap the repository call in try/catch and return `null`

questions.explanation: Nest 500s anything that isn't an `HttpException` — correctly, since unknown errors must not leak. The fix is to map the *expected* condition at the layer that understands it and rethrow the rest. Mapping every error to 409 lies to clients; swallowing it hides the failure; a DTO validator races the write (only the unique index actually prevents the duplicate).

questions.prompt: Why is Nest's rate limiter a *guard* rather than an interceptor?

options.text: Rate limiting is an admit/reject decision — a guard's whole contract — and guards run before every interceptor, so a throttled request is turned away before that work starts
Guards run after validation, so requests that fail the pipes never count against the limit
An interceptor would also count requests the pipes are about to reject with a 400; a guard doesn't
Only guards can set response headers

questions.explanation: Rate limiting is an admit/reject decision, which is a guard's entire contract. Guards also run before every interceptor (and a global guard before the controller- and route-level guards, such as a token check), so a throttled request is turned away before that work starts. Both tempting reasons get the order wrong: guards run *before* pipes, so a guard-based limiter counts malformed requests exactly as an interceptor would — which is what you want from a rate limiter anyway. And interceptors can set headers too.

prompts.prompt: An API-key guard that can't fail open: the interface it implements, and what it returns when no key is configured.
prompts.explanation: Without the `if`, an unset `API_KEY` makes the last line compare `undefined === undefined` for any request that omits the header — `true`, so the guard admits everyone. A comparison-based check must first confirm it has something to compare against, and refuse when it doesn't (`false` → 403). Better still, validate `API_KEY` at boot so the app won't start without it, and keep this line as the backstop.

prompts.prompt: Read route metadata set by a custom `@Roles()` decorator, letting the handler override the controller.
prompts.explanation: `getAllAndOverride` returns the first match in the array, so handler metadata wins over class metadata (`getAllAndMerge` unions them instead). The decorator itself is just `SetMetadata(ROLES_KEY, roles)` — configuration as data on the route, not an `if` inside the guard.

prompts.prompt: Wrap every successful response in `{ data }` — the operator that replaces the value, applied to the handler's stream.
prompts.explanation: `next.handle()` is the handler, as an Observable, and you must return it: Nest subscribes to what `intercept()` returns, so returning nothing gets the client a 500 and the handler never runs. `map` transforms the emitted value; `tap` would only observe it and leave the response unchanged.

prompts.prompt: Record the duration whether the handler succeeded or threw.
prompts.explanation: `finalize` runs on completion, error, and unsubscribe — the right operator for metrics and cleanup. `tap(fn)` covers only the success notification, so it silently drops exactly the requests you most wanted to measure.

prompts.prompt: Register a global exception filter that needs an injected logger.
prompts.explanation: `useGlobalFilters(new DomainErrorFilter())` takes an instance you construct outside any module, so the injector supplies nothing. The `APP_FILTER` token (like `APP_GUARD`, `APP_INTERCEPTOR`, `APP_PIPE`) registers it as a provider, so the injector builds it.

prompts.prompt: Handle only your domain error type in this filter, leaving everything else to Nest's default.
prompts.explanation: `@Catch(DomainError)` narrows the filter; a bare `@Catch()` catches everything and then owns the entire error contract, including the shapes Nest was formatting for you. Only one filter runs per exception: the first match, checking route-level filters, then controller-level, then global.

code: // Registered globally, in this order: LoggingInterceptor, AuthGuard, LogPipe.
create(@Body() dto: CreateOrderDto) {   // one argument, so the pipe runs once
snippets.question: In what order do the five logs appear for one successful request?
acceptable: guard, pre, pipe, handler, then post
snippets.explanation: The pipeline is guards → interceptors(pre) → pipes → handler → interceptors(post) → filters, whatever order you registered them in — registration order only matters among components of the same kind. Note what that means in practice: an interceptor's pre-handler code has already run by the time a pipe rejects the request with a 400. (Pipes run per argument: a handler taking both `@Param()` and `@Body()` would log `pipe` twice.)

code: export class AuditInterceptor {          // no `implements NestInterceptor`, so this compiles
// Bound with @UseInterceptors(AuditInterceptor) on GET /orders; no custom filters.
snippets.question: What does the client get for `GET /orders`, and does the handler run?
snippets.answer: A 500 Internal server error, and the handler never runs
snippets.explanation: Nest subscribes to whatever `intercept()` returns, merging it into the response stream with RxJS. `undefined` isn't a stream, so that throws `TypeError: You provided 'undefined' where a stream was expected`, and the default filter turns it into a logged, generic 500 (Nest 11 and 12) — not a hang. Meanwhile `next.handle()` was never subscribed, so the handler never ran and `done` never prints. With `implements NestInterceptor` the class wouldn't compile: the interface requires `intercept()` to return an `Observable` (or a `Promise` of one).

code: if (hit) return of(hit);          // never calls next.handle()
// Inside it: a handler-level interceptor that logs "inner-pre", a ValidationPipe, the handler.
snippets.question: On a cache hit, which of "inner-pre", the pipe's validation, and the handler run?
snippets.explanation: Everything inside the pipeline is downstream of `next.handle()`. Skipping that call skips the inner interceptors, the pipes and the handler entirely — which is the point of a cache, and also why an unvalidated cache key is a security bug: nothing else got a chance to check the request.

code: // No custom exception filter is registered.
snippets.question: What status code and body does the client receive?
snippets.answer: 500 with a generic "Internal server error" — the message is not exposed
snippets.explanation: Nest's default filter only formats `HttpException` subclasses; anything else is treated as an unexpected failure, logged, and reported as a generic 500 so internal details don't leak. Throw `ConflictException("order already closed")` — or map `OrderClosedError` in a `@Catch(OrderClosedError)` filter — to make it a 409 with a real message.
